name: Reissner-Nordström Charged Black Hole
description: The unique static, spherically symmetric vacuum solution to the Einstein-Maxwell equations describing the spacetime exterior to a charged mass that does not rotate.
convention: The parameter $r_s = 2GM/c^2$ is the Schwarzschild radius, and $r_q^2 = Q^2 G / (4\pi\epsilon_0 c^4)$ is the square of the charge radius, where $Q$ is the total electric charge. The Ricci tensor is the standard contraction, $R_{\mu\nu} = R^\alpha{}_{\mu\alpha\nu}$.
history: The charged generalization of the Schwarzschild metric arrived in pieces, and the story parallels the uncharged case almost beat for beat. In May 1916, Hans Reissner gave the gravitational field of a point charge, solving the Einstein equations in the presence of a Coulombic electric field [reissner1916]. His derivation used Schwarzschild's auxiliary radius $R$, so the solution was not yet in its modern form, and its singularities were interpreted in the same auxiliary radius that had hidden the structure of Schwarzschild's. Gunnar Nordström was himself no stranger to the problem of gravity: his scalar theory of gravitation had been a serious contender before Einstein's field equations settled the matter in 1915.¶Nordström turned to the victorious theory anyway, and in 1918 did for Reissner's metric what Johannes Droste had done for Schwarzschild's: imposing isotropy directly on the auxiliary radius, he extended the areal coordinate to $r = 0$, giving the solution its modern form [nordstrom1918]. Hermann Weyl had arrived at the same metric independently in 1917, as one member of a broad class of static fields in which the gravitational and electrostatic potentials depend on one another [weyl1917, bicak2000]. George Barker Jeffery derived it again in 1921, solving the field equations directly for the field of an electron, and learned of Nordström's work only after his own paper was written [jeffery1921].¶The metric is characterized by two length scales: the Schwarzschild radius $r_s = 2GM/c^2$ and the charge radius, defined by $$r_q^2 = \frac{Q^2 G}{4\pi\epsilon_0 c^4},$$ where $M$ is the mass and $Q$ the electric charge of the source. The metric admits up to two horizons, located at $$r_\pm = \frac{r_s}{2} \pm \sqrt{\frac{r_s^2}{4} - r_q^2}.$$ These coalesce when $r_s = 2r_q$ in the extremal case, and become imaginary when the ratio of charge to mass exceeds $\sqrt{4\pi\epsilon_0 G}$. Nordström noted that the ratios of charge to mass of the proton and electron far exceed this threshold, and used this to argue that the regime beyond extremality represents elementary charged particles, elegantly banishing the horizons by phenomenological fiat. It wouldn't be until decades later that the case beyond extremality was understood as a naked singularity, a violation of cosmic censorship [misner1973].¶John Graves and Dieter Brill gave the analytic extension of the charged metric in 1960 and found it unlike Kruskal's: the throat of the charged wormhole contracts to a least radius and expands again after a finite proper time, pulsating, cushioned by the Maxwell pressure of the electric field through it, and no uncharged test particle can reach the singularity at $r = 0$ [graves1960]. Brandon Carter completed the extension in 1966 for the extremal case, where the charge equals the mass [carter1966]. Sudhansu Datta Majumdar generalized Weyl's work in 1947 to static fields in which the metric and the electrostatic potential are tied by a single relation, which reduces the field equations to Laplace's equation [majumdar1947], and James Hartle and Stephen Hawking showed in 1972 that such solutions extend analytically to extreme charged black holes held in equilibrium by the balance of gravity and electricity [hartle1972]. Werner Israel proved in 1968 that among static electrovacuum fields that are asymptotically flat, with closed, simply connected equipotential surfaces, the only ones with a regular event horizon are the Reissner-Nordström solutions whose mass is at least as large as their charge in natural units [israel1968].¶The Ricci scalar vanishes identically for this metric, yet the Ricci tensor is nonzero: the spacetime is sourced entirely by the energy and momentum of the electromagnetic field. The Reissner-Nordström metric is the unique static, spherically symmetric solution to the Einstein-Maxwell equations, and Einstein and Rosen later applied the same trick of extending the domain to it as they had to the Schwarzschild metric, interpreting the two sheets of the geometry as positive and negative particles. Vincent Moncrief showed in 1974 that the coupled gravitational and electromagnetic perturbations of even parity outside a Reissner-Nordström black hole have no unstable normal modes [moncrief1974].¶Michael Simpson and Roger Penrose found in 1973, from computer calculations of test electromagnetic fields, that instabilities arise at the inner horizon though not at the event horizon, and inferred that in the full theory the inner horizon becomes a curvature singularity once perturbations without symmetry are present [simpson1973]. Eric Poisson and Werner Israel made the mechanism explicit in 1989 and 1990: the slowly decaying radiative tail of a collapse is blueshifted without limit at the inner horizon and inflates the internal mass parameter of the hole without bound, while the mass seen from outside stays finite, which they called mass inflation [poisson1989, poisson1990]. Mihalis Dafermos proved in 2005 that their picture is right for a spherical charged black hole coupled to a scalar field: the spacetime extends continuously across a boundary on which the Hawking mass blows up, so it cannot be extended as a differentiable metric, and in Demetrios Christodoulou's formulation by continuous extension the strong cosmic censorship conjecture fails for that system [dafermos2005].

related.text: The black hole with no charge, $r_q = 0$, and with it no inner horizon.
The charged black hole set spinning. With $a = 0$ Kerr-Newman is Reissner-Nordström.
The throat of the extremal black hole, $r_q = r_s/2$. In the limit taken toward its horizon the geometry is AdS$_2 \times$ S$^2$ [gibbons1993].

Any number of extremal Reissner-Nordström black holes at rest together, the electric repulsion of each pair balancing its gravity. James Hartle and Stephen Hawking showed in 1972 that these solutions are black holes [hartle1972].
The charged black hole of low energy string theory, where a scalar field couples to the Maxwell field. It has one horizon for every charge [garfinkle1991, horowitz1992].
Reissner-Nordström is a Malament-Hogarth spacetime, as John Earman and John Norton noted in 1993 [earman1993].

The charged black hole in a universe with a positive cosmological constant. A cosmological horizon joins the two of Reissner-Nordström, and at $r_q = r_s/2$ it has the temperature of the black hole horizon [romans1992].
A regular black hole with the same tower of universes, two horizons to each black hole, and another asymptotically flat region where this one has its timelike singularity [simpson2019].
Reissner-Nordström with the singularity taken out. James Bardeen put in place of $1 - r_s/r + r_q^2/r^2$ a function that is regular at $r = 0$, and kept both horizons [borde1994].
A black hole with the same two horizons and the same tower of regions, and a regular centre at $r = 0$ [hayward2006].

The rotating black hole, which has an inner horizon too and no spherical symmetry. Eric Poisson and Werner Israel worked out mass inflation in 1989 on a charged spherical hole as a model of the inside of a spinning one [poisson1989, poisson1990].
A pair of black holes accelerating apart. William Kinnersley and Martin Walker gave them a charge in 1970, in a solution that generalises Reissner-Nordström's [kinnersley1970].

A star that shines, Schwarzschild's metric with a mass that changes in retarded time. William Bonnor and Prahlad Vaidya gave it a charge in 1970, the radiating form of Reissner-Nordström's metric [bonnor1970].
Einstein and Nathan Rosen's particle of 1935. Its charged bridge is this metric continued to $r_q^2 \to -r_q^2$, which leaves one horizon at any mass, even none [einstein1935].
The charged black hole in anti-de Sitter space. At fixed charge its small and large black holes are like the liquid and the gas of a van der Waals fluid [chamblin1999].

Reissner-Nordström with its mass and its charge carried in or out by charged light. William Bonnor and Prahlad Vaidya made both functions of a null time in 1970, and with both held constant their metric is Reissner-Nordström's [bonnor1970].
A black hole whose metric function takes any power of $r$ where Reissner-Nordström's has the charge's $1/r^2$. The charge term is its case $w = 1/3$ with the sign reversed [kiselev2003, visser2020].

The same hole with radiation crossing its interior. Eric Poisson and Werner Israel sent two streams of light through it in 1989 and found the mass function growing without limit at the inner horizon [poisson1989].

Give every point a small circle and twist it by the potentials of equal electric and magnetic charges, and Reissner and Nordström's black hole solves the vacuum equations of five dimensions [larsen2000].

Balls of Yang-Mills field with a regular centre and no horizon, one for each number $n$ of zeros of the field. In the limit $n \to \infty$ their outside is the extreme hole, $r_q = r_s/2$, with a magnetic charge [breitenlohner1994, volkov1999].
One moment of two charged black holes at rest, each with a throat like the one on the slice $t = 0$ of Reissner and Nordström's hole [brill1963].

coordinates.name: Spherical
coordinates.convention: The coordinate $r$ is the areal radius. We take the region between the horizons $r_\pm = \dfrac{r_s}{2} \pm \sqrt{\dfrac{r_s^2}{4} - r_q^2}$ to be the black hole. We work in units with $c = 1$ throughout and take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, which is then $t$ itself, so $t$ is a length beside $r$, $r_s$, and $r_q$.
coordinates.line_element: ds^2 = -\dfrac{r^2 - r_s r + r_q^2}{r^2}\,dt^2 + \dfrac{r^2}{r^2 - r_s r + r_q^2}\,dr^2 + r^2 d\Omega^2
geodesics: \ddot{r} + \dfrac{(r^2 - r r_s + r_q^2)(r r_s - 2r_q^2)}{2r^5}\dot{t}^2 - \dfrac{r r_s - 2r_q^2}{2r(r^2 - r r_s + r_q^2)}\dot{r}^2 - \dfrac{r^2 - r r_s + r_q^2}{r}\dot{\theta}^2 - \dfrac{r^2 - r r_s + r_q^2}{r}\sin^2\theta\,\dot{\phi}^2 = 0
